summary:
Perm Krai is a federal subject of Russia and stands under the national framework set out in the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment updated 11 June 2025). In Russia, same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections apply.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. The expanded 'propaganda' law criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. It carries administrative fines, and repeat offences are punishable by up to four years in prison.

The Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in 2023. Participating in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten; Human Rights Watch states that participants face up to 12 years in prison.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism convictions tied to the designation as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison. In the same period 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office note records that between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

Foreign nationals who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly advise LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has expanded sharply in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the preceding two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation, and characterised arrests, club raids and extremism charges as defining LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Residents of Perm Krai live under the same statutory regime as the rest of Russia: administrative liability for propaganda offences, criminal liability for participation in or organisation of the designated extremist movement, and no legal pathway to change a gender marker or access gender-affirming care through the health system.

Survey data cited in the UK Home Office note show respondents in the Volga area, the federal district containing Perm Krai, were more 'closeted' toward relatives than the whole-study sample, indicating a higher level of concealment within families than in the study population overall.

Displaying symbols alleged to belong to the designated movement is prosecuted as an administrative offence under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses; 81 people were found guilty on that basis across 98 cases between January 2024 and June 2025. Criminal participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment, and organisation six to ten.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people across Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. The inventory provides no Perm Krai-specific breakdown of that figure.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement actions taken specifically within Perm Krai: no documented raids, prosecutions or administrative cases there. The national figures cited apply to Russia as a whole.

The exact statutory provision behind the 'up to 12 years in prison' figure attributed to participants in the designated movement is not identified in the inventory; the same note separately gives two to six years for participating and six to ten for organising.

Access to documentation, facility rules and street-level treatment for transgender visitors in Perm Krai are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

The conversion-therapy detention described by BBC Russian occurred near Novosibirsk, in Siberia, and cannot be read as evidence of conditions in Perm Krai.

The UK Home Office note's Volga-area survey finding covers the wider federal district rather than Perm Krai alone; its wording, publication and the identity of the underlying survey are unresolved from this inventory.
